books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: Federal Reserve Bulletin, September 1937, Table 1 (bank suspensions, 1921-1936)

stimulus.text:
| Year | Banks that closed |
| 1929 | 659 |
| 1930 | 1,350 |
| 1931 | 2,293 |
| 1932 | 1,453 |
| 1933 | 4,000 |

Bank suspensions in the United States, 1929–1933. The 1933 figure counts banks closed in the banking crisis and not licensed to reopen after the March 1933 bank holiday.
stimulus.source_note: Figures from the Federal Reserve Bulletin, September 1937, Table 1 (bank suspensions, 1921–1936).

source: original; stimulus table built from Federal Reserve Bulletin, September 1937, Table 1
stem: The pattern in the table is best explained by which of the following?

options.text: The government closed healthy banks to punish speculators
options.misconception: The government did not close healthy banks. Banks closed because they could not meet withdrawals or repay loans.

options.text: Farmers repaid their loans early as crop prices rose
options.misconception: Crop prices fell in the 1920s, they did not rise. Farmers fell behind on loans, and rural banks failed.

options.text: New banks opened faster than old banks closed
options.misconception: If new banks had outpaced closures, the banking system would have grown. Instead thousands closed and credit dried up.

options.text: Rumors of failure caused runs that closed even sound banks

rationales.A: Background from the books: banks failed when they could not weather panic withdrawals, not because the government punished them.
rationales.B: Background from the books: farm prices collapsed after World War I, and 6,200 rural banks failed in the 1920s as farmers could not repay.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the table counts closures, and the Depression saw the banking system shrink, not grow.
rationales.D: Background from the books: runs on banks began with rumors that a bank was failing, and customers rushed to withdraw savings, so even banks that might have survived were drained and failed.
rationales.general:
1. Read the pattern: closures climb steeply after 1929.
2. Ask what closes banks so fast. Background from the books: rumors set off runs, and runs drain a bank's cash.
3. Ask whether only weak banks fell: runs could close even sound ones.
4. Rumors and runs best explain the pattern.
Remember: a bank run is a panic about a bank, so ask what fear does to a bank's cash.
